common_name: Variegated Cretan Brake Fern (Silver Ribbon Fern)

planting.note: Divide crowded clumps in spring and pot into a loose, humus-rich mix; outdoors it can be set in a shaded bed after the last frost in warm zones, but elsewhere it is grown year-round as a houseplant.

directions: This variegated sport of the Cretan brake fern carries a bold silvery-white stripe down the center of each narrow, ribbon-like pinna, contrasting against grey-green margins in a way the plain species lacks. It is native, like the species, to open woodland and rocky slopes across the Mediterranean, Asia, and Africa, and stays evergreen where winters stay above roughly 10 to 15 degrees F, dying back in colder gardens. Grow it as a houseplant in bright indirect light and even moisture almost everywhere in the U.S., or tuck it into a shaded, frost-sheltered bed on the Gulf Coast, where its clean variegated foliage brightens deep shade under trees or on a covered porch. Its slow-clumping habit and light-catching stripe make it a long-time favorite for terrariums, dish gardens, and mixed shade containers.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

common_name: Wilson's Crested Brake Fern (Club Foot Fern)

planting.note: Divide rooted offsets in spring and pot into fast-draining, humus-rich potting mix; treat as an outdoor plant only in mild, frost-protected shade gardens.

directions: Also sold as the club foot or fan table fern, this compact Cretan brake fern cultivar produces fronds whose pinnae fan and crest at the tips into small clustered crowns, quite unlike the plain straplike leaflets of the wild species. Like other Pteris cretica forms, it traces back to open, humid woodland habitats spanning the Mediterranean basin through tropical Asia, and it survives outdoors only where winters stay mild. Its low, dense, ruffled-looking mound suits terrariums, shaded rock gardens in frost-free climates, and shady windowsills, where the crested texture reads almost moss-like from a distance. Keep it out of direct sun and let the growing medium approach dryness between waterings to avoid crown rot.

planting.note: Divide small offsets in spring into shallow pots of rich, well-drained soil; this dwarf form is grown almost exclusively as an indoor or terrarium plant north of the Gulf Coast.

directions: This refined selection of the silver lace fern, first developed in Evergem, Belgium, stays notably smaller and more finely cut than the straight species, with slender, deeply lobed fronds bearing a bright silvery-white band down the center of each leaflet. Like the species, it descends from tropical brake ferns native to Asia and the Pacific, and it needs warmth and steady humidity to thrive, making it unsuited to outdoor culture outside the warmest, most sheltered Gulf Coast gardens. Its small scale and delicate, feathery texture make it a favorite for closed terrariums, bottle gardens, and dish gardens, where the metallic stripe catches light beautifully against surrounding green foliage. Divide congested clumps rather than trying to grow it from spores, since named color forms do not come true from spore propagation.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

common_name: Deer's Foot Fern (Canary Island Hare's Foot Fern)

planting.note: Set rhizome sections onto the surface of a shallow, fast-draining, humus-rich mix in spring, leaving the furry rhizomes exposed to the air rather than buried, the same way the species grows over rocks and tree bark in habitat.

directions: Native to the Canary Islands, Madeira, and the western Mediterranean, this fern is named for its thick, creeping rhizomes covered in silvery-brown scales that fan out visibly across the growing medium or over a hanging basket's rim like a small animal's paw. It is somewhat more cold-tolerant than the tropical Fijian and squirrel's foot ferns already common in cultivation, going deciduous and dying back to the rhizome in a cool winter before resprouting the following spring. Grow it mounted on bark, in a shallow basket, or over rock in bright, humid shade, and let the surface dry slightly between waterings since the fleshy rhizomes store moisture and rot if kept constantly wet. Its architectural, exposed-rhizome habit makes it a conversation piece distinct from the finely divided fronds of most other shade ferns.

planting.note: Divide rooted crowns in spring into rich, well-drained potting mix; grown as a houseplant or hanging-basket fern nearly everywhere, with only the warmest frost-free gardens able to keep it outdoors year-round.

directions: A compact sport of the classic Boston fern, 'Teddy Junior' forms a tight, dense rosette of curled, tightly overlapping pinnae on short arching fronds, staying far more restrained than the sprawling species or 'Bostoniensis' and shedding fewer of the wiry runners that make full-size Boston ferns messy indoors. New fronds emerge a fresh lime green and darken as they mature, giving the mound a two-toned look. Its small, tidy scale suits hanging baskets, tabletop pots, and mixed shade containers on porches and patios where a full-size Boston fern would sprawl too far, and it needs consistently moist soil and high humidity to keep its fine texture from browning. Like other Nephrolepis exaltata cultivars, it descends from a pantropical wetland and swamp species and will not come true from spores, so division of the crown is the only reliable way to propagate it.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Divide small offsets in spring into rich, moisture-retentive potting mix; this compact cultivar is grown as a houseplant, terrarium fern, or hanging-basket specimen rather than a landscape plant outside the tropics.

directions: This Dutch-bred Boston fern cultivar is one of the smallest named forms in cultivation, with tightly ruffled, densely packed light-green pinnae on short fronds that give the whole plant a thickset, lacy appearance rather than the long trailing fronds of the species. It shares the wetland and swamp-forest origins of Nephrolepis exaltata across the tropics and subtropics, and it needs steady warmth, humidity, and moisture, never tolerating nighttime temperatures much below 55 degrees F. Its small mature size makes it especially well suited to closed terrariums, bottle gardens, and bathroom or kitchen windowsills where humidity naturally runs high, filling a niche the larger Boston fern cultivars cannot. Divide congested crowns to propagate, since this cultivar will not breed true from spores.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Divide rooted crowns in spring into rich, moisture-retentive potting soil; grown outdoors year-round only in frost-free zones, and otherwise as a houseplant or seasonal porch and hanging-basket fern.

directions: An heirloom Boston fern cultivar dating back to the early twentieth century, 'Whitmanii' bears fronds so finely and repeatedly divided that they take on a soft, feathery, almost cloud-like texture quite different from the broader pinnae of the species or 'Bostoniensis'. It shares the same pantropical wetland ancestry as other Nephrolepis exaltata forms and depends on consistently high humidity to keep its delicate, lacy foliage from browning at the edges. Its cascading, fine-textured fronds have long made it a favorite for large hanging baskets and pedestal urns on shaded porches, where its old-fashioned, Victorian-parlor look stands apart from the coarser modern Boston fern selections. Propagate only by dividing the crown, since named lacy-leaf sports do not reproduce true from spores.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Pot offsets or nursery starts into loose, well-drained, humus-rich mix in bright indirect shade; grown outdoors year-round only in frost-free tropical zones, and as a houseplant everywhere else.

directions: This compact selection of the Japanese bird's nest fern produces glossy, undivided fronds with strongly wavy, crimped margins that curl and ruffle around a central rosette, giving each plant a crown-like symmetry more pronounced than the flatter fronds of the wild species. Native populations of Asplenium antiquum occur epiphytically on trees and rock in humid forests of Japan and East Asia, and the plant needs warmth and high humidity to hold its form well. Its dramatically ruffled, sculptural foliage makes it a striking accent for shaded lanais, covered porches, and container groupings in frost-free gardens, and a long-lived tabletop or floor houseplant elsewhere. Water at the soil line rather than into the central crown, since standing water in the rosette invites rot.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Pot nursery divisions into loose, well-drained, humus-rich mix in bright indirect shade; treat as a container or houseplant fern outside the warmest frost-free tropical gardens.

directions: One of a group of newer bird's nest fern selections bred for novelty foliage, 'Crissie' produces glossy, gently undulating fronds that branch and crest at their tips, forking into small forked crowns instead of tapering to a plain point as in the species. Like other Asplenium nidus forms, it grows naturally as an epiphyte on trees and rock outcrops across tropical Asia, Australia, and the Pacific, drawing moisture and nutrients from leaf litter caught in its rosette. Its open, somewhat larger habit compared to similar crested selections makes it well suited to 5 to 8 inch pots as a specimen houseplant or shaded patio accent in warm climates. Keep the potting mix evenly moist and humidity high, and avoid letting water sit in the central crown to prevent rot.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox
